To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the no b‐wave phenotype is not always indicative of the absence of the On pathway, as was previously assumed.
the b‐wave ERGs of mice with mutations in genes that are expressed by DBCs, such as Grm6, are absent.
the no b‐wave phenotype is not indicative of a single retinal circuit defect, and that the b‐wave can be generated by a variety of different mechanisms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of visual signal transduction in the retina and the role of specific genes in this process.
elucidating the mechanisms that control retinal development, and how these are disrupted in retinal diseases.
the identification and characterization of genes involved in the visual system, with a particular focus on genes that are involved in the transmission of visual signals through the DBCs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single retinal phenotype that is associated with the absence of a functional b‐wave.
the b‐wave phenotype is not a reliable predictor of the underlying retinal circuitry.
there are at least two different types of congenital stationary night‐blinding phenotypes, one that affects both On and Off pathways and another that affects primarily the Off pathway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the b‐wave phenotype is the result of a lack of output from the DDCs, but the mechanism of how this occurs is not necessarily a lack of On pathway input.

the b‐wave phenotype can be caused by a number of different mutations that affect the retina in a number of different ways, and that the b‐wavelength ERG phenotype is not a reliable indicator of a lack of On pathway signalling.

(a) the no b‐wave phenotype is not indicative of a lack in On pathway output; (b) the b‐wave phenotype may be caused by different mutations that have very different effects on the retina and (c) the no b ‐wave phenotype may be a result of the mutation and/or the genetic background of the animal.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the no b‐wave phenotype does not necessarily indicate a loss of the On pathway, and therefore, the no b‐waves phenotype alone cannot be used as a predictor of the functional outcome in human patients.
the ERG b‐wave phenotype does not necessarily reflect a loss of the On pathway, and that the ERG phenotype should be interpreted in light of other functional and structural data.
the ERG b‐wave is a complex waveform that is not simply a reflection of DBC activity.
